tokens.c: That being said we can also have a more refined assessment of their effect downtown with the tools at hand. By creating a filter of 0.7 miles from a proposed NTOR location, specifically Broadway and 6th, we can isolate the locations in that area of downtown. In total, there were 444 reported accidents within 50 feet of a crosswalk. Here are the results.

body.caption: Figure 4: Reported Incidents (Fuchsia) with Pedestrians, Cyclist, and E-Scooter-Type Transportation Within 50 Ft of Proposed NTOR Signage (Teal), Filtered for Proximity to NTOR in Downtown Nashville
body.description: Figure 4: Reported Incidents (Fuchsia) with Pedestrians, Cyclist, and E-Scooter-Type Transportation Within 50 Ft of Proposed NTOR Signage (Teal), Filtered for Proximity to NTOR in Downtown Nashville

tokens.c: There are multiple proposed NTOR signage sites with 2, 3, 4, even 5 reported incidents. Here are just a few examples:

items: Broadway and 10th Ave S.: 5 incidents
Broadway and Rosa Parks: 6 incidents
Broadway and 7th Ave S: 4 incidents
John Lewis and Demonbreun St: 3 incidents
John Lewis and Korean Veterans Blvd: 5 incidents
Korean Veterans and 4th Ave S.: 4 incidents

tokens.c: And on, and on, and on.

So, yes, even with this limited data, these 59 NTOR signage locations seem to be good, targeted policy despite the whining from downtown business interests who would like to get to work in their automatic Porsche Cayenne just a fraction of their time faster. The better question is, does this go far enough? If not, what intersections should be targeted for Phase 2? Well, expanding the view to include all crosswalks, you tell me…

body.caption: Figure 5: Reported Incidents (Fuchsia) with Pedestrians, Cyclist, and E-Scooter-Type Transportation Within 50 Ft of Crosswalks (Goldenrod) or NTOR Signage (Teal)
body.description: Figure 5: Reported Incidents (Fuchsia) with Pedestrians, Cyclist, and E-Scooter-Type Transportation Within 50 Ft of Crosswalks (Goldenrod) or NTOR Signage (Teal)

tokens.c: This view doesn’t even include all the locations, but there are 594 incidents that took place within 50 feet of a crosswalk or proposed NTOR signage (118 on average per year). With 146 of them within proposed NTOR signage alone, there are 448 incidents (~90 incidents a year) that took place outside of proposed NTOR locations in Phase 1 but within proximity to a crosswalk that could be possible candidates for Phase 2. And, again, I can’t stress this enough, that this is from limited MNPD-reported data alone.
But let’s look at downtown Nashville again.

body.caption: Figure 6: Reported Incidents (Fuchsia) with Pedestrians, Cyclist, and E-Scooter-Type Transportation Within 50 Ft of Crosswalks (Goldenrod) or NTOR Signage (Teal), Filtered for Proximity to NTOR in Downtown Nashville
body.description: Figure 6: Reported Incidents (Fuchsia) with Pedestrians, Cyclist, and E-Scooter-Type Transportation Within 50 Ft of Crosswalks (Goldenrod) or NTOR Signage (Teal), Filtered for Proximity to NTOR in Downtown Nashville

tokens.c: Look at all the accidents at crosswalks where there is no proposed NTOR signage.
What strikes me immediately is Lower Broadway on the right. Several goldenrod dots, many many fuchsia, and no teal. Some examples:

items: Broadway and John Lewis: 5 incidents
Broadway and 4th: 10 incidents
Broadway and 3rd: 6 incidents

tokens.c: And that’s just Lower Broadway.
Looking outside of specific intersections and at the broader picture, here is a breakdown of total accident data, injury data, and fatalities for those outside of a car within 50 feet of a crosswalk:

items: As a reminder, there are a total of 1,286 reported accidents represented here.
594 (46%) of accidents with pedestrians, cyclists or other non-motor vehicles occurred within 50 ft of a crosswalk.

581 of those 594 incidents resulted in injuries, with many being multiple individuals, with 47% of total incidents with injuries occurring 50 ft from a crosswalk compared to those that weren’t. In total, 630 people were injured 50 ft from crosswalks.

15 (2.5%) incidents of those 594 resulted in fatalities (all individual deaths) with 26% of total deaths (58) occurring 50 ft from crosswalks. 3 of those 15 deaths (20%) occurred at proposed NTOR signage.
123 (21%) accidents of the 594 were within 50ft of a crosswalk were at the proposed NTOR signage.

tokens.c: And here is that same breakdown, but filtered for proximity to the proposed NTOR in downtown Nashville alone.

items: With this filter, there are 444 reported accidents represented.
276 (62%) of accidents with pedestrians, cyclists or other non-motor vehicles occurred within 50 ft of a crosswalk.

272 of those 276 incidents resulted in injuries, with many being multiple individuals, with 62% of total incidents with injuries occurring 50 ft from a crosswalk compared to those that weren’t. In total, 295 people were injured 50 ft from crosswalks.
9 (3.3%) incidents of those 276 resulted in fatalities (all individual deaths) with 56% occurring 50 ft from crosswalks. 3 of those 9 deaths (33%) occurred at proposed NTOR signage.
111 (40%) accidents of the 276 within 50 ft of a crosswalk were at the proposed NTOR signage in downtown Nashville alone.

tokens.c: Let’s compare this accident data in downtown to that within 50 feet of all crosswalks

items: There are 444 reported accidents in downtown compared to 1,286 for all crosswalks. 35% took place downtown.
For all accidents involving pedestrians, cyclists or other non-motor vehicles within 50 ft of a crosswalk, 276 took place downtown compared to 594. 46% occurred downtown.
9 such accidents occurred downtown compared to 15 within all crosswalks. 60% occurred downtown.
111 accidents occurred at a proposed NTOR signage downtown compared to 123 at all NTOR signage. That’s 90%.

tokens.c: As mentioned, this data was also calculated for incidents within 100 feet of proposed NTOR signage and crosswalks. For the sake of length, I will leave the reader to review the maps and full data breakdowns on the Tableau Public dashboards, but here are the bullet points:

items: Total number of accidents represented remains the same: 1,286
716 (56%) of accidents with pedestrians, cyclists or other non-motor vehicles occurred within 100 ft of a crosswalk within these parameters.
698 of those 716 incidents resulted in injuries with 57% of incidents with injuries occurring at 100 ft from crosswalks. In total, 761 people were injured within 100 ft of a crosswalk.
20 (2.7%) of those 716 resulted in fatalities with 34% occurring 100 ft from crosswalks. Those same 3 deaths of 20 (15%) occurred at proposed NTOR signage.
The number of accidents within 100 ft of NTOR is the same, so 123 (17%) of the 716 accidents within 100ft of a crosswalk were at the proposed NTOR signage.

tokens.c: In short, the naysayers are wrong and they, frankly, are selfish in their reasoning. They are more worried about congestion, that is, their own convenience, rather than their community’s safety when the data clearly shows there will be a demonstrable positive impact for those walking and riding the streets outside of a personal vehicle.

Here, I’m estimating between a 17-21% reduction in accidents at crosswalks involving pedestrians, cyclists and people on other alternative forms of transportation such as e-scooters at the proposed NTOR crosswalks based on MNPD’s accident data alone. In downtown alone, that figure doubles to around a 40% reduction.
It is quite likely then that the before-and-after accident figures at these proposed NTOR locations would be much higher, and NTOR pilots in other cities back this up.
A pilot to restrict RTOR in Washington, DC decreased vehicle-pedestrian and vehicle-vehicle conflicts by 92% and 97% respectively.

q.web-byt44: “Vehicle to Vehicle conflicts were nearly eliminated, showing a 97 percent reduction following NTOR implementation. … Failure to Yield to Pedestrians (Red Interval): 166 → 13 (−92%). Vehicle-Vehicle Conflict (Red Interval): 124 → 4 (−97%).” — DDOT’s before/after evaluation of the 2019 100-intersection RTOR ban (before: Feb–Mar 2019; after: Apr–May 2019; 74 of 100 locations with both-period data; 252 approaches). The same study reported crosswalk encroachment rose ~30%; the after-window was ~2 months. Corroborated by the DC Council committee report on the citywide ban (LIMS 48835, fn 8).
q.web-byt35: “Additionally, a recent study published by the Institute of Transportation Engineers lists that NTOR signage can reduce pedestrian-vehicle conflicts by 92% and vehicle-vehicle conflicts by 97% during the red interval at signalized intersections.” (Citing ITE, Analysis of Expanded No Turn on Red Applications, May 2022 — i.e., DDOT’s pilot evaluation, see [26].)

tokens.c: Similar results were found in a San Francisco pilot.

“Vehicles blocking or encroaching onto crosswalks on a red signal was reduced by more than 70%.”

According to an early assessment of the program from the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency, the ban reduced the number of “close calls.” The agency found that about 92% of vehicles were observing the rule, and the number of cars blocking crosswalks during a red light decreased by 70%.”

tokens.c: Furthermore, when right on red was legalized 50 years ago in response to the 1970s gas crisis, pedestrian and cyclist involved crashes increased by 43–107% and 72–123% respectively at the studied sites after RTOR adoption — real jumps, but on a small base: RTOR accidents were between 1% and 3% of all pedestrian or bicycle accidents, and about 0.05% of all crashes, though they are a larger share of pedestrian crashes at signalized intersections.

tokens.c: I mean, c’mon….
It’s just not a debate anymore. The data is just not on the side detractors. It wasn’t when right on red was first introduced 50 years ago and it’s not today.

CM Sepulveda is right. NDOT is right. The big whiny boo boo boss babies downtown are wrong and no amount of special community meetings for them to share their big strong feelings on the matter will make them right.
Period. End of Story. So it’s time to turn the page on the matter.

operand.headline: By the Numbers: No Turn on Red, Nashville Safety, and Big Boss Babies Downtown
operand.dek: What Metro’s own crash data shows about No Turn on Red in Nashville — intersection by intersection.

tokens.c: Last Tuesday, September 22nd, I attended a community meeting downtown at Cannery Hall to review the substitute text for BL2026-1497.

q.web-byt5: “Much of the discussion at Tuesday night’s community meeting at Cannery Hall focused on how the intersections were chosen, and what the city’s crash data can prove.”
q.web-byt6:
“Metro Council deferred second reading of a bill to restrict right on red, pending a community meeting.”
“Councilmember Jacob Kupin, who represents the downtown area where most of the identified intersections are, was advocating for a deferral. Sepulveda moved to defer … and the two will hold a community meeting about the proposal on Sept. 22.”
“NDOT Deputy Director Brad Freeze said there have been at least 22 pedestrian injuries and one fatality related to right-on-red since the start of 2025.”
q.web-byt1: “Except as described otherwise in section 12.12.200, the Nashville Department of Transportation and Multimodal Infrastructure is authorized to determine those intersections at which drivers of vehicles shall not make a right or left turn or U-turn, and shall place proper signs at such intersections.” — §1 (12.12.030)

tokens.c: This bill, which was originally broader in scope, but then limited after receiving feedback as well as the seal of approval from the Nashville Department of Transportation (NDOT), includes a plan to roll out No Turn on Red (NTOR) signage for high incident intersections in phases.

q.web-byt2: “The original version of BL2026-1497 called for the Nashville Department of Transportation and Multimodal Infrastructure to place “No Turns On Red” signs at all signalized intersections within Nashville’s Urban Services District … Metro’s analysis identified 744 signalized intersections in the Urban Services District. … after discussions with NDOT and review of the proposal, a substitute takes a more targeted approach. Instead of immediately applying the restriction across the Urban Services District, the revised plan starts with 59 signalized intersections. Most of those intersections are downtown, while others are near places such as schools, parks and hospitals. … The substitute gives NDOT three months to install or modify signage at the initial 59 locations.”

tokens.c: The first phase is relatively immediate with 59 intersections, the majority of which is in the downtown core, giving particular attention to common spaces such as schools and hospitals.

q.web-byt2: “The original version of BL2026-1497 called for the Nashville Department of Transportation and Multimodal Infrastructure to place “No Turns On Red” signs at all signalized intersections within Nashville’s Urban Services District … Metro’s analysis identified 744 signalized intersections in the Urban Services District. … after discussions with NDOT and review of the proposal, a substitute takes a more targeted approach. Instead of immediately applying the restriction across the Urban Services District, the revised plan starts with 59 signalized intersections. Most of those intersections are downtown, while others are near places such as schools, parks and hospitals. … The substitute gives NDOT three months to install or modify signage at the initial 59 locations.”

tokens.c: There is also a follow-up phase directing NDOT to evaluate additional signalized intersections in the Connect Downtown footprint, NashvilleNext Tier 1 zones, and within 500 feet of school zones — WSMV reports 89 school-adjacent signals and 297 Tier 1 intersections (386 total), and NDOT’s Derek Hagerty told the meeting it is about 200 additional intersections.

q.web-byt20:
“1. Identify and evaluate all signalized intersections within: the footprint described in the Connect Downtown Action Plan …; the Tier 1 zone of the NashvilleNext general plan …; and the areas within 500 feet of a school zone.”
“within three months following the effective date of this section, NDOT shall install or modify traffic control devices and signage at 59 signalized intersections identified in the attached exhibit.”
q.web-byt4:
“The new proposal is based around the Connect Downtown and NashvilleNext plans that have already completed traffic studies at 59 intersections in busy areas.”
“NDOT engineers would then start collecting data and completing traffic studies over 9 months for the 89 traffic lights within 500 feet of Metro Nashville Public Schools and the 297 intersections identified as ‘Tier 1 zones’ in NashvilleNext.”
q.web-byt21:
“Derek Hagerty, with the Nashville Department of Transportation, said in the 59 intersections they are studying, there have been 18 crashes over the past five years involving a right-turning vehicle and a pedestrian.”
“Hagerty said the resolution also includes a study of 200 additional intersections in areas with a lot of pedestrian traffic.”

Using Metro Nashville’s Open Data Portal and the Council’s Legistar portal, a few key, though imperfect, data points can be collected:

q.web-byt41: 220,478 records, 2019-01-01 → 2026-09-09. Re-run 2026-10-04: zero bicycle records; rolling-5-year pedestrian (2,207) + “other non-motorist” (147) = 2,351 (calendar-2021→now = 2,636). The export is an incomplete subset of MNPD’s data: in MNPD’s own window (2025-01-01→2026-08-03) it yields 591 pedestrian-injury incidents vs MNPD’s published 664 (−11%) and 0 bicycle-injury vs 164. MNPD’s published countywide figures (664+164 in 19.5 months ≈ 2,541 in five years) match the author’s 2,560 (95%) at 100.7% — the portal simply does not publish the disaggregated bicycle/person-type data. The 50/100/1,000 ft geospatial breakdown is not re-derivable from this export alone.

items.c: Traffic incident data from the Open Data Portal that includes pedestrians, cyclists, and “other type non-motorist,” which seems to include methods such as e-scooters given their prevalence in mid-town, downtown, and East Nashville.

items: Crosswalk locations from the Open Data Portal, which, while imperfect, are a useful proxy to look at the Urban Services District as that is primary area they cover.

items.c: Proposed NTOR signage locations as mentioned in BL2026-1497 from Legistar, Metro Nashville’s depository for council legislation.

tokens.c: A few caveats, the data NDOT analysts would have access to would be much more refined than just what is available via Metro Nashville Police Department (MNPD) accident records on the Open Data Portal. They appeared to include a technical form of “conflict” that included but also went beyond reported incidents with MNPD. It also should be mentioned that crosswalks are not the same as intersections as all intersections can be crossed but may not have dedicated crosswalks. In addition to point number three made above, crosswalks provide a useful point on a map for geospatial analysis. There are probably others I’m not privy to as I don’t work in NDOT or with their data, but, again, this is to see if this moves us in their direction.

For an initial pass, this information was plotted in Google Maps. One set looked at all MNPD reported incidents, of which there were 2,679. For a sense of comparison, another Google Map was created where an injury or fatality was involved with 2,560 incidents (or 95%) reported by MNPD. This is helpful for a high-level overview, sense of scale, and for poking around on a map, but it doesn’t get to the question of if NTOR is warranted both at these initial 59 locations in Phase 1 or beyond for Phase 2. To do so, we would need link the proximity of MNPD reported accidents to the proposed NTOR signage as well as other crosswalks in Nashville.

web-byt2.title: Nashville drivers react as ‘no right on red’ proposal gets scaled back
web-byt2.text: “The original version of BL2026-1497 called for the Nashville Department of Transportation and Multimodal Infrastructure to place “No Turns On Red” signs at all signalized intersections within Nashville’s Urban Services District … Metro’s analysis identified 744 signalized intersections in the Urban Services District. … after discussions with NDOT and review of the proposal, a substitute takes a more targeted approach. web-byt14.title: D.C. Law 24-214 — Safer Streets Amendment Act of 2022
web-byt14.text: “Beginning January 1, 2025, a motor vehicle operator shall not make a turn when facing a steady red traffic control signal unless DDOT has installed signage … permitting a turn when facing a steady red traffic control signal at that intersection.”

web-byt38.title: No turn on red light law to be implemented at DC intersections
web-byt38.text: “107,353 traffic crashes occurred in the District from 2013-15, yet making a right turn on red was a factor in only 55 of them.”

web-byt34.title: Tenderloin No Turn on Red Evaluation — factsheet
web-byt34.text:
“close calls for vehicle-pedestrians decreased from 5 close calls before NTOR signs were posted to 1 close call after restrictions were in place at observed intersections.”
“Vehicles blocking or encroaching onto crosswalks on a red signal was reduced by more than 70%.”
“On average, 92% of vehicles are complying.”
“In San Francisco, turn on red crashes account for less than 1% of all injury crashes.”

web-byt12.title: San Francisco could ban right turns on red. Could L.A. soon follow?
web-byt12.text:
“In the fall of 2021, San Francisco banned right-hand turns on red lights in more than 50 intersections of the Tenderloin neighborhood. According to an early assessment of the program from the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency, the ban reduced the number of “close calls.” The agency found that about 92% of vehicles were observing the rule, and the number of cars blocking crosswalks during a red light decreased by 70%.”
“Right-hand turns on red lights came to be through the 1975 Energy Policy and Conservation Act, which required states to allow the turns to receive federal funding.”

web-byt15.title: The Effect of Right-Turn-on-Red on Pedestrian and Bicyclist Accidents
web-byt15.text: “Many states adopted Western RTOR in the mid-1970’s. … Measures of pedestrian and bicycle accidents involving a motorist making a right turn at a signalized location increased significantly at all study sites after the adoption of Western RTOR. Estimates of the magnitude of the increases ranged from 43% to 107% for pedestrian accidents and 72% to 123% for bicyclist accidents. … These RTOR accidents constituted between 1% and 3% of all pedestrian or bicycle accidents in the studied locations.” (The ROSAP abstract page says 48–107%; the report body and Addendum say 43–107% — the report’s own figure is used here.)

web-byt13.title: D.C. Passes Bill To Ban Right Turns At Red Lights, Implement ‘Idaho Stop’ For Cyclists
web-byt13.text:
“Turning right on red first became widespread in the United States during a fuel shortage in the 1970s.”
“The District banned the practice at 100 dangerous intersections in 2019. A study found that it made intersections safer and resulted in generally reduced conflicts between pedestrians and vehicles.”

web-byt39.title: Safety Impact of Permitting Right-Turn-On-Red — A Report to Congress
web-byt39.text: “RTOR crashes represent a very small proportion of the total number of traffic crashes in the four states (0.05 percent)… RTOR injury and fatal crashes represent a fraction of 1 percent of all fatal and injury crashes (0.06 percent)… RTOR crashes represent a very small proportion of signalized intersection crashes (0.4 percent).” (Correction: previously attributed to Zador 1982; this is NHTSA’s 1994 report to Congress, Compton & Milton. Zador, Moshman & Marcus 1982 separately reported ~21% more right-turning crashes and +57% urban pedestrian crashes.)

web-byt24.title: Right turn on red debate draws questions from Nashville residents
web-byt24.text:
“Williams said throughout the county from the start of 2025 through Aug. 3, 2026, there were just four crashes involving a pedestrian or bicyclist being hit by a driver reported at intersections where turning right on red is already forbidden, compared to 49 at intersections where right turns on red are permitted.”
“The latest turn in the debate was a Sept. 22 community meeting at Cannery Hall, hosted by downtown council member Jacob Kupin and District 32 council member Sandra Sepulveda, the bill’s main sponsor.” (Note: Legistar and nashville.gov list Sepulveda as District 30; the Tennessean’s “District 32” is a typo.)
“Sepulveda told the room that with 28 pedestrians and bicyclists dead after being struck by drivers in Nashville this year to date, and another more than 300 left seriously injured, she thought something needed to happen to stop the trend.”

web-byt25.title: Enforcement questions remain on ‘no turn on red’
web-byt25.text: “According to the Metro Nashville Police Department, there have been roughly 50 pedestrian crashes involving cars turning on red, including one fatality, since 2025.”

web-byt19.title: San Francisco Moves to Ban Right Turns on Red
web-byt19.text: “SFMTA’s own evaluation showed that 92% of drivers complied with NTOR, close calls decreased by 80%, and drivers blocking crosswalks decreased 72% after SFMTA implemented NTOR at 50 intersections in the Tenderloin in 2021.”

web-byt23.title: Nashville Scene — Metro Council right-on-red, Donelson call center
web-byt23.text: “NDOT would continue studying more than 700 areas.”

web-byt36.title: ITE Informational Report IR-151-E — Prohibition of Turns on Red at Signalized Intersections
web-byt36.text: State-of-practice survey + literature summary (July 2022). The 92%/97% figures cited here trace to DDOT’s pilot evaluation published in ITE Journal (May 2022) — see [26]; IR-151-E is not their origin.

web-byt37.title: Traffic Signals Safe Streets Act of 2023 — experience page
web-byt37.text: “A pilot project in the District of Columbia found ‘decreased overall right turn conflicts between pedestrians and vehicles across the study intersections’ but did not quantify the crash reduction.”

web-byt40.title: Review of Pedestrian Safety Research (FHWA-RD-03-042)
web-byt40.text: RTOR is “a small but clear safety problem for pedestrians”; “21% of motorists violate NTOR signs, 23% of violations produce a conflict.”

web-byt42.text: 1,823 records; fields Inspector, AuditDate, FeatureType, Width, CrossSlope, PaintCondition, AssetID.
